summary: Login slowness and 503s on auth-service trace to auth-service itself becoming CPU-saturated: aggregate CPU stepped from a ~34-40% baseline to ~96-97% at ~06:52 in the same 2-minute bucket that request_rate first upticked (from a flat ~400 req/s), with p99 inflecting one bucket later at 06:54 (90 ms -> 3.76-3.88 s), all 64 workers saturated (queue 39035) and 'accept queue full' 503s on /v1/auth/login from 06:55:42. Every measured dependency candidate is exonerated as an origin: redis-cache and its three co-consumers plus the only service deployed this week (portfolio-service) are flat across onset; user-db is flat on cpu/lag/slow-queries/disk through 06:51 with connections_active rising only after auth onset; api-gateway degrades 3-4 minutes later with no resource saturation of its own. The reporter's bcrypt-regression framing is not supported - there was no auth-service deployment in the entire week (F10) and no bcrypt signature in the logs (F7). The best-supported origin is therefore an in-process per-request CPU-cost increase inside auth-service (H1, confidence 0.45) on an unchanged workload, but because the trigger is unidentified and the CPU-vs-request-rate ordering cannot be resolved below 2 minutes, H1 does not cross the 0.50 threshold and the outcome is honestly inconclusive.

ranked_hypotheses.title: auth-service CPU saturation from a rise in per-request compute cost (no tracked change; bcrypt framing unsupported)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service itself became CPU-bound at ~06:50-06:52: its aggregate CPU stepped from a flat ~34-40% baseline to ~97% while inbound request_rate was still at baseline (~400 req/s, 452 at 06:50), i.e. CPU/request cost rose rather than load rising first. All 64 workers saturate (queue 39035), the accept queue fills and returns 503 on /v1/auth/login, and accepted requests wait behind the saturated pool (p99 ~90 ms -> 3.8 s). The origin is inside auth-service's request-handling path. The trigger is genuinely unknown: no auth-service deploy or meaningful config change exists in the week, so the cost increase must come from an untracked change (in-flight code, feature flag, request-mix/JWT-size change, or an injected per-request work path) or from an in-process pathology (retry spin, lock contention, GC) that presents as CPU. The bcrypt framing of the original report is NOT supported (F7: no bcrypt signature; F10/F11: no auth-service release), so the mechanism is 'CPU cost per request rose', cause unidentified.

causal_chain.claim: auth-service CPU steps from ~34.4% (06:50 bucket) to 96.89% (06:52 bucket) while inbound request_rate is still baseline (452.43 at 06:50) — cost per request rose on a flat workload
At ~97% CPU all 64 workers are occupied and the internal queue grows to 39035
The accept queue overflows, so the listener returns 503 on /v1/auth/login (first at 06:55:42); error rate settles at ~14%
Requests that are accepted wait behind the saturated pool, pushing p99 from ~90 ms to ~3.8 s (inflection 06:54 bucket)

Elevated request_rate (742 at 06:52 -> 1749 at 06:58) and rate_limited_per_min (1.2 -> 451 at 06:54) are consequences — retries/backlog against an already-slow service — and the HPA cap (desired 14 > maxReplicas 8) prevents scaling out of it

assumptions: The CPU is consumed by auth-service's own request path (per-request compute) rather than by an in-process stall that presents as CPU (spinning retry loop, lock contention, GC).
Some untracked change or request-mix shift raised per-request CPU cost; no tracked deploy/config event explains it (F10, F11).
The 2-min bucket resolution does not hide a request_rate rise in the tens of seconds immediately before the CPU step; F25 accepts this cannot be excluded below 2 minutes.
Aggregate CPU across the 8-replica cap is representative of per-pod cost; no per-pod series exists.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Capacity ceiling: login demand outran auth-service's provisioned concurrency with no faulty change
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The origin is demand plus a provisioning ceiling rather than a change: a login-traffic surge hit auth-service, whose autoscaler is capped (autoscaler message 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further'). With fixed capacity and 64 workers/pod, the worker pool and accept queue saturate, producing ~3.8 s p99 and 503s, and ~97% CPU is the expected consequence of running at provisioned capacity. This differs from H1 in origin (demand vs. per-request cost) and in fix (raise the replica/pool ceiling and/or rate-limit the surge vs. find the code path that got more expensive).

causal_chain.claim: Login request volume surges, visible as rate-limited requests climbing from ~2/min to 487 (06:51) and ~900/min (07:00+)
The autoscaler cannot absorb the surge: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8, so no additional capacity is added
Fixed worker capacity (64/64) is exhausted and the internal queue grows to 39035, driving CPU to ~96-97%
The accept queue fills and returns 503 on /v1/auth/login; queued requests see multi-second p99 (~90 ms -> 3.8 s)

assumptions: The surge is exogenous (real or synthetic login flood) and not itself produced by clients retrying an already-slow service.
The maxReplicas=8 ceiling is genuinely binding — F6 quotes the HPA message but no replica/time series was retrieved.

A ~400 req/s workload could not, by itself, have been at 38% CPU a minute earlier if the surge were the sole cause; this hypothesis must assume a much larger effective concurrency than the measured request_rate suggests, or that request_rate is under-reported.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Dependency-first degradation on auth-service's synchronous login path (user-db, kyc-provider, or api-gateway path)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Something on auth-service's synchronous login path degraded first and auth-service queued on it, saturating its worker pool and accept queue. The tested shared components are exonerated (redis-cache flat CPU 21.5% and hit ratio 95.9% at onset; its three co-consumers and portfolio-service all flat), so the remaining untested candidates are user-db (the login path's datastore; only proxy metrics exist — connections_active, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min, disk_used_pct) and the external kyc-provider (has_telemetry=false, unmeasurable). This is the orchestrator's 'victim' theory, now narrowed to the components that were never measured.

causal_chain.claim: user-db or kyc-provider on the login path degrades at or just before onset
auth-service's synchronous calls block, consuming all 64 workers and growing the internal queue
Worker pool saturation persists without a strong CPU-bound signature in logs, and p99 rises to ~3.8 s in the 06:51 bucket
The saturated/queued service overflows the accept queue and returns 503; request_rate and rate-limit counters then climb as clients retry

assumptions: user-db could have degraded in a way its flat proxy metrics (replication_lag_ms 27.65-32.31, cpu_pct 16.6-19.9, slow_queries 0.18-0.51, disk 43.4-44.9) would not show — e.g. a latency/IOPS or connection-pool wall on the auth path.
kyc-provider is called synchronously on /v1/auth/login and could be slow/failing; it has no telemetry at all (has_telemetry=false).
Blocking on a dependency can drive auth-service CPU to 97% (e.g. retry spin, TLS/JSON rework on retries); otherwise the flat, saturated CPU signature favours an in-process cause.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reporter's prior-incident mechanism: bcrypt cost regression from an auth-service release
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A release of auth-service raised the bcrypt cost factor (as in HIST-101, 2025-08-14), making each login hash far more CPU-expensive; CPU saturates, workers queue, and the accept queue returns 503. Retained as the reporter's explicit suspicion, but its stated prerequisite — an auth-service release — is falsified by the deployment inventory.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service release raising the bcrypt cost factor is deployed before onset
Login hashing becomes CPU-bound, driving CPU to ~97%
Worker pool saturates (64/64, queue 39035) and the accept queue returns 503
p99 rises to ~3.8 s and error rate to ~14%

assumptions: The tracked deployment inventory is incomplete (off-list or un-tracked code change) — directly contradicted by F10.
The bcrypt signature would not necessarily appear as an explicit log line.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F10 shows exactly one deployment in the entire 2026-04-15..2026-04-22 window and it is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z, not auth-service; F11 shows the only config change is a log-level INFO->WARN tweak three hours before onset. HIST-101's stated prerequisite (an auth-service release) is absent, and F7 finds no bcrypt or panic signature in the WARN/ERROR set. F12 is a past-incident precedent and weak evidence on its own. H3 is kept rejected; the surviving CPU-cost mechanism (H1) is deliberately re-framed without asserting bcrypt or a deploy.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency rose from a ~89-90 ms baseline (05:30-06:42) to 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket and held ~3.78-3.88 s through 08:57; onset is between 06:42 and 06:51.
auth-service error_rate was 0.18-0.25% through 06:42, spiked to 7.88% in the 06:51 bucket, and settled at ~14% from 07:00 onward.
The first 503 on /v1/auth/login is logged at 06:55:42 as 'accept queue full, returning 503'; the immediately preceding WARN at 06:54:53 is 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)'.
auth-service CPU jumped from ~38% (05:30-06:42) to 89.96% avg (max 97.33) in the 06:51 bucket and stayed ~96-97% through 08:57.
auth-service memory stayed flat at ~51-53% and restarts were 0 for the entire window, so this is not a memory-driven crash or pod restart.
There was NO auth-service deployment between 2026-04-15 and 2026-04-22; the only deployment in that week is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z.
The only config change in the 2026-04-15..2026-04-22 window is cfg-2801 on auth-service: log.level INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z.
Precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14) is the prior bcrypt regression (cost factor 10->14 in release v6.4.0); its prerequisite - an auth-service release - is absent in the current window.
auth-service's dependency graph: outgoing edges to user-db (db), redis-cache (cache), kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry=false); api-gateway has an http edge INTO auth-service.
redis-cache is a shared datastore consumed by four services: auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service.
redis-cache showed no degradation at onset: CPU averaged 21.55% in the 06:51 bucket vs 22.33% at 06:42 and 22.14% at 07:00.
redis-cache showed no cache-storm or capacity signature at onset: hit_ratio_pct stayed 95.86% in the 06:51 bucket and evictions_per_min stayed ~3/min, matching pre-onset values.
portfolio-service - the only service deployed this week and a co-consumer of redis-cache - shows no latency change at onset: p99 avg 180.28 ms in the 06:51 bucket vs 180.46 ms at 06:42.
The other two shared-redis consumers are also flat across onset: pricing-engine p99 avg 59.66 ms and market-data-service p99 avg 40.17 ms in the 06:51 bucket, both unchanged from 06:42.
user-db does not expose latency_p99_ms; its available metrics are connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min.
The metric backend returns auth-service sub-buckets at bucket_seconds=120 (2-min resolution); all four series share that grid with missing_points=0 and partial=false.

auth-service inbound request_rate was flat at ~381-418 req/s for the entire baseline 06:00-06:48; at the 06:50 bucket it was still only 452.43 avg and it inflected upward only in the 06:52 bucket (742.81), reaching 1350.36 at 06:56 and peaking 1749.75 avg at 06:58.

auth-service per-service CPU jumped FIRST, in the 06:52 bucket (96.89% avg / 96.96% max) from a flat ~34-40% baseline; the CPU step and the request_rate step (742.81) land in the SAME 2-min bucket, so request rate did not precede CPU.

The p99 latency inflection is in the 06:54 bucket (3759.86 ms avg), AFTER both the CPU step and the request_rate step; the 06:50-06:52 buckets were still baseline-fast (93.94 ms avg at 06:50, 91.5 ms avg at 06:52).
rate_limited_per_min was flat ~1.3-2.6 req/min through 06:52, then rose sharply at 06:54 (451.86 avg), lagging rather than leading the CPU step.
user-db connections_active was flat (22.79-27.75) through the auth-service onset, then jumped to 72.59 at 06:52 - one bucket AFTER auth-service's 06:51 onset.

user-db's other four metrics are flat across onset: replication_lag_ms 27.65-32.31, cpu_pct 16.63-19.94%, slow_queries_per_min 0.18-0.51, disk_used_pct 43.41-44.87 - no saturation, lag spike, slow-query burst or disk exhaustion at or before 06:51.

api-gateway was flat through the auth-service onset and only degraded at 06:54 (~3 minutes later): latency_p99_ms held 198.84-226.13 ms for 06:30-06:53 then leapt to 4024.51 at 06:54; error_rate stepped from 0.11-0.31% to 9.4% at 06:55.
api-gateway showed no resource saturation as trigger: cpu_pct stayed 36.92-45.98% for the entire window including the 4024 ms latency bucket, never approaching saturation.

Rate-limiting on auth-service rose from ~2 req/min baseline to 487 in the 06:51 bucket and ~900 req/min (max 979.25) from 07:00 on, alongside an autoscaler message 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further'.

assumptions: The CPU is consumed by auth-service's own request path (per-request compute) rather than by an in-process stall that presents as CPU (spinning retry loop, lock contention, GC).
Some untracked change or request-mix shift raised per-request CPU cost, since no tracked deploy or config event explains it (F10, F11).
The 2-min bucket resolution does not hide a request_rate rise in the tens of seconds immediately before the CPU step; this cannot be excluded below 2 minutes (F20, F25).
Aggregate CPU across the 8-replica cap is representative of per-pod cost; no per-pod series exists.
kyc-provider is called synchronously on /v1/auth/login and could be slow/failing, but it has no telemetry at all (has_telemetry=false) so this was never directly measured (F8).

user-db could have degraded in a way its flat proxy metrics (replication_lag, cpu_pct, slow_queries, disk) would not show - e.g. a latency/IOPS or connection-pool wall on the auth path - since it exposes no latency_p99_ms (F19, F28).

The user-db connections_active jump at 06:52 is a downstream consequence (auth-service opening more/retrying connections) rather than an independent db-side saturation; the 06:52 timestamp supports this but a pool-limit check was not retrievable.

The so-called api-gateway degradation is propagation of auth-service slowness rather than a gateway-local event; this rests on metrics-only ordering (latency 06:54, errors 06:55 vs auth p99 onset 06:51 and first 503 06:55:42) without gateway logs (F29, F30, F31).

The metric backend's 2-min resolution and the absence of any earlier inflection in the 06:30-06:51 stretch for the measured neighbours is sufficient to treat the dependency-first candidates as not supported; no bucket earlier than 06:30 was inspectable (F26).
The recorded maxReplicas=8 ceiling is genuinely binding; the HPA message is quoted but no replica/time series was retrieved (F6).

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) No bcrypt/CPU-regression or panic signature appears in the auth-service WARN/ERROR set; observed patterns are queue/pool saturation, accept-queue-full 503s, one /internal/metrics slow request, and an NTP clock-drift message.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) No dependency latency rise precedes or coincides with auth-service's onset: shared redis-cache, its three co-consumers, and portfolio-service all remain at baseline in the 06:42 and 06:51 buckets while auth-service p99 rose.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Interpretation of the H1-vs-H2 test: request_rate did not rise before the ~38%->~97% CPU jump within 2-min resolution; the elevated inbound rate is best read as retry/backlog consequence of the already-slow service, consistent with H1 and not explained by H2's pre-onset surge premise.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The api-gateway deviation sequence (latency 06:54, errors 06:55) lines up with and follows auth-service's own saturation evidence (p99 2532 ms at 06:51; first accept-queue-full 503 at 06:55:42), consistent with the gateway propagating slowness/503s from auth-service.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Relevant precedents for auth-service slowness that do NOT involve an auth-service release are HIST-107 (cold cache storm after redis failover) and HIST-110 (datastore IOPS throttling).

timeline.event: Only config change in the week: cfg-2801 on auth-service, log.level INFO->WARN by config-bot. Three hours before onset.
Baseline: auth-service p99 ~89-90 ms (through 06:42), CPU ~38%, request_rate ~381-418 req/s.
portfolio-service v4.4.0 deployed - the only deployment in the entire 2026-04-15..04-22 window; it remains flat across onset.
auth-service request_rate still essentially baseline at 452.43 avg (max 529.5); p99 still baseline-fast at 93.94 ms.

auth-service p99 jumps to 2532 ms; error_rate spikes to 7.88%; CPU bucket averages 89.96% (max 97.33). Dependency candidates (redis-cache, its three co-consumers, portfolio-service) all remain at baseline in this bucket.

auth-service CPU steps to 96.89% avg in the per-service series, in the SAME 2-min bucket that request_rate first upticks to 742.81 - CPU did not follow a prior request-rate rise. user-db connections_active simultaneously jumps from ~26 to 72.59, i.e. after auth onset.
auth-service p99 inflects to 3759.86 ms avg; rate_limited_per_min rises to 451.86; api-gateway p99 simultaneously leaps to 4024.51 ms with its CPU only 39.4%.
auth-service WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' - all 64 workers saturated, 39035 queued.
api-gateway error_rate steps from ~0.2% to 9.4%, consistent with propagating auth-service 503s.
First 503 logged on /v1/auth/login: 'accept queue full, returning 503'; becomes the top ERROR pattern (372 occurrences).
auth-service request_rate peaks at 1749.75 avg as retries/backlog accumulate against the saturated service.
Sustained failure: error_rate ~14%, rate_limited_per_min ~900 (max 979.25), with autoscaler message 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further'.
Incident INC-008 reported by on-call SRE as login latency ~4s and 503s, suspected bcrypt regression.
CPU remains 96.6-98.8%; p99 held ~3.55-3.93 s through this point and ~3.78-3.88 s through 08:57.
Latest data; auth-service still CPU-saturated (~96-97%), p99 ~3.8 s, error_rate ~14%. Memory flat and restarts 0 throughout.

recommended_actions.action: Mitigate on the auth-service side now: shed or throttle inbound load at the edge for /v1/auth/login and/or add capacity to auth-service (raise the autoscaler maxReplicas above the recorded maxReplicas=8 cap, or raise the per-pod worker pool above 64) to drain the 39035-deep worker queue and clear the accept-queue-full 503s.
recommended_actions.rationale: The verified failure chain is auth-service-local: CPU 34-40% -> 96.9%+, 64/64 workers saturated with queue 39035, accept-queue-full 503 on /v1/auth/login, p99 90 ms -> 3.8 s. Capacity was the binding constraint on absorbing the load, and the autoscaler itself reported it could not scale further (F4, F3, F6, F22). SPOF caution: raising the replica ceiling only masks a per-request CPU-cost problem, so pair it with the short-term diagnosis below.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back auth-service expecting a bcrypt fix, and do not attribute this to a bad auth-service deploy: confirm that no auth-service release exists in the window before choosing a rollback target.
recommended_actions.rationale: The report's premise is falsified: the only deployment in 2026-04-15..2026-04-22 is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z, and the only config change is a log-level INFO->WARN tweak at 03:40Z (F10, F11). No bcrypt signature appears in the WARN/ERROR set (F7). Rolling back a non-existent auth-service release is not actionable.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT apply a mitigation based on redis-cache, user-db, or api-gateway as the origin (e.g. cache warm/failover actions from HIST-107, or DB connection-pool changes) as the first-line fix.
recommended_actions.rationale: All measured dependency candidates are victims, not origin: redis-cache CPU/hit-ratio/evictions flat across onset; its three co-consumers and portfolio-service flat; user-db flat on cpu/lag/slow-queries/disk through 06:51 with connections_active rising only after auth onset; api-gateway degrades 3-4 min later with CPU only 37-46% (F14, F15, F16, F17, F18, F27, F28, F29, F30, F31).

recommended_actions.action: Discriminate the trigger inside auth-service's request path: pull the auth-service change/flag history and in-flight code state (feature flags, traffic-shadowing, request-mix and JWT-size distribution), and capture a CPU profile or flame graph of a saturated pod to identify which request-handling code path became more expensive per request.
recommended_actions.rationale: The origin is inside auth-service's request-handling path on an unchanged ~400 req/s workload (F21, F22, F25), but the trigger is genuinely unknown - no tracked deploy or config change exists in the week (F10, F11). Profiling is the direct test of H1's mechanism and is the only way to name the exact expensive path.

recommended_actions.action: Instrument and verify saturation recovery: add per-pod CPU, accept-queue depth, and worker-pool occupancy as exposed time series for auth-service, then confirm after mitigation that queue depth drains, p99 returns to the ~90 ms baseline, error_rate returns to ~0.2%, and rate_limited_per_min returns to ~2/min.
recommended_actions.rationale: Accept-queue/worker-pool occupancy exist only in log messages, not as metrics, and CPU is aggregate-only, so the saturation cannot be plotted against onset (F3, F20, F25). Verified recovery requires the same signals that failed here, and low rate_limited/error values are the observable definition of resolved (F2, F6, F24).

recommended_actions.action: Close the observability gaps on the unmeasured dependencies: add telemetry to kyc-provider (currently has_telemetry=false) and add latency/error series to redis-cache and user-db on the login path so future auth-service incidents can be resolved dependency-first or not.
recommended_actions.rationale: kyc-provider and parts of the user-db path could not be measured at all, and redis-cache exposes no latency/error metric - so H4's remaining candidates were never directly falsified by latency, only by proxy and by temporal ordering (F8, F19, F26).

recommended_actions.action: Add a workload-independent guard on per-request compute cost: track and alert on CPU-per-request (or queue depth per unit of sustained inbound rate) for auth-service, and require a change/flag audit step before any auth-service release, to catch an untracked per-request cost increase before it saturates the worker pool.
recommended_actions.rationale: H1's mechanism is a rise in CPU cost per request at unchanged load (F21, F22, F25); a CPU-per-request SLO would have fired at the 06:52 CPU step, well before the 06:55:42 accept-queue-full 503. An untracked change is the leading explanation for the trigger (F10, F11).

data_gaps: Neighbouring-service correlation is unanswered: 'user-service' returned not_found (not in known_services) and the session-service query plus remaining calls hit the tool-call budget, so it cannot be confirmed or denied that auth-service is the only affected service.

No per-pod CPU series exists for auth-service (available_metrics has only aggregate cpu_pct), so the 38%->97% jump cannot be attributed to individual pods versus an aggregate of the 8-replica cap; this also means H1 (all pods' per-request cost rose) cannot be distinguished from a pods-count effect.

No accept-queue-depth or worker-pool-occupancy time series is exposed for auth-service; those quantities exist only in log messages, so their timing relies on log first-seen times rather than metric buckets and cannot be plotted against onset at 2-min resolution.

The finest available granularity is bucket_seconds=120; a request-rate rise within tens of seconds before the 06:52 CPU step is not ruled out, so the H1-vs-H2 temporal precedence is only established at 2-minute resolution.

No metric bucket earlier than 06:30 was retrieved for user-db or api-gateway (budget exhausted), so a pre-06:30 inflection in either component cannot be excluded by direct measurement; the flatness claim is bounded to 06:30-06:51/06:54.

api-gateway and user-db WARN/ERROR logs, api-gateway request_rate/memory_pct/restarts, and user-db connection-count limits were not retrievable (budget_exhausted), so it cannot be confirmed from logs whether the gateway's 06:54 latency jump is propagated auth-service slowness versus a gateway-local event, nor whether the user-db connection jump at 06:52 is a pool-limit saturation.

api-gateway exposes no connection/queue-count metric, so gateway accept-queue pressure - the closest analogue to auth-service's 'accept queue full' - is unmeasurable and a queue-level gateway origin cannot be evaluated.

kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry=false) has no telemetry, so its latency/error contribution to login was never measurable; redis-cache exposes no latency/error metric, so its health is inferred only from CPU/hit-ratio/eviction proxies.

Deployment/config changes on the shared components themselves (user-db, redis-cache) beyond their appearance in the service-level lists were not checked, and no rollback/restart/flag events for redis-cache were returned, so a redis failover/replica event (the HIST-107 mechanism) around onset cannot be confirmed or excluded.

The exact minute of the p99 inflection is not pinned down (bounded by the 9-minute baseline 06:42 and elevated 06:51 buckets); no sub-bucket zoom was run and no auth-service tracing or release event was pulled.

The precise trigger of the CPU cost increase is unidentified: no profiling, no feature-flag audit, and no request-mix/JWT-size distribution exists, so the mechanism is stated only as 'CPU cost per request rose, cause unidentified'.

Lateral impact paths through user-db (shared-postgres enumeration) and api-gateway dependencies were not mapped (get_service_dependencies run only for auth-service and redis-cache), so a neighbour damaging auth-service through the user DB or the gateway cannot be ruled out.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that a dependency on the login path degraded BEFORE 06:51 (e.g. a kyc-provider slowdown, or a user-db latency/IOPS or connection-pool wall masked by its flat proxy metrics) would move the conclusion to a dependency-first origin (H4) and change the fix to that component.

A sub-2-minute series showing request_rate rising before the CPU step (rather than stepping in the same 06:52 bucket) would support H2's demand-surge/capacity-ceiling reading and change the primary fix to rate-limiting/raising the replica ceiling rather than the auth-service code path.

Discovery of an auth-service deployment, feature-flag flip, or in-flight code change in the window would restore a change-triggered origin (and, if a bcrypt cost increase were found, H3) - none currently exists in the tracked inventory.

A CPU profile or flame graph showing the CPU is consumed by an in-process stall (spinning retry loop, lock contention, GC) rather than per-request compute would invalidate H1's stated mechanism while leaving the saturation chain intact.

Evidence of a redis-cache failover or replica event around onset (the HIST-107 mechanism) would reopen the shared-component hypothesis, since redis exposes only CPU/hit-ratio/eviction proxies and no failover events were retrieved.
Log evidence showing api-gateway errors originated locally (rather than propagating auth-service 503s) would make a gateway-side origin viable; currently only metrics-only ordering is available.
Any auth-service-side change mitigation (throttle/capacity) that fails to restore p99 and drain the worker queue would falsify the auth-service-local origin and point elsewhere.

findings.statement: auth-service p99 latency rose from a ~89-90 ms baseline (05:30-06:42) to 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket and held ~3.78-3.88 s through 08:57, so onset is between 06:42 and 06:51.
auth-service error_rate was 0.18-0.25% through 06:42, then spiked to 7.88% in the 06:51 bucket (max 14.76) and settled at ~14% (max 15.67) from 07:00 onward.

First 503 on /v1/auth/login is logged at 06:55:42 as 'accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)'; the immediately preceding WARN at 06:54:53 is 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)'. Top ERROR pattern (372 occurrences) is the accept-queue-full 503.

auth-service CPU jumped from ~38% (05:30-06:42) to 89.96% avg (max 97.33) in the 06:51 bucket and stayed ~96-97% through 08:57 — a sharp, sustained CPU saturation coincident with the latency/error onset.
auth-service memory stayed flat at ~51-53% for the entire window and restarts were 0 throughout, so the failure is not a memory-driven crash or pod restart.

Rate-limiting on auth-service rose from ~2 req/min baseline to 487 in the 06:51 bucket and ~900 req/min (max 979.25) from 07:00 on, alongside an autoscaler message 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' — indicating demand/connection pressure the service could not scale out of.

findings.statement: No bcrypt/CPU-regression or panic log signature appears in the auth-service WARN/ERROR set; the observed log patterns are queue/pool saturation (worker pool saturated active=64/64), accept queue full 503s, one /internal/metrics slow-request, and an NTP clock-drift message — the evidence points to saturation, not an explicit bcrypt message.

findings.statement: auth-service's dependency graph: outgoing edges to user-db (db), redis-cache (cache), kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry=false); api-gateway has an http edge INTO auth-service. No edge to a separate session/token store or secrets service was returned.

redis-cache is a SHARED datastore (shared:true) consumed by four services: auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service — so a change or degradation in redis-cache or in any neighbouring consumer can affect auth-service login.

There was NO auth-service deployment between 2026-04-15T00:00Z and 2026-04-22T09:00Z: the deployment list for that whole week contains exactly one entry, portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z (status live, rolled_back_at null). This contradicts the report's premise of an auth-service release.

The only config change in the 2026-04-15..2026-04-22 window is cfg-2801 on auth-service: log.level INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ("Reduce log volume"). Nothing else changed in config across all services.

Precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14) is the prior bcrypt regression and the basis for the report's guess: symptoms 'login p99 4s, 503 on login, high cpu', root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. Its prerequisite is an auth-service release, which is absent in the current window (finding above).

findings.statement: Relevant precedents for auth-service slowness that do NOT involve an auth-service release: HIST-107 (2025-12-09) 'Cold cache storm after redis failover' on redis-cache/market-data-service, root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica', resolution 'Warmed cache; fixed replica sync checks'; and HIST-110 (2026-01-15) latency from datastore IOPS throttling. Both are infrastructure/datastore-side leads matching the shared redis-cache path.

findings.statement: redis-cache showed no degradation at onset: CPU averaged 21.55% in the 06:51 bucket vs 22.33% at 06:42 and 22.14% at 07:00 (window mean 22.02%, max 25.59), i.e. flat through the auth-service onset.

redis-cache showed no cache-storm or capacity signature at onset: hit_ratio_pct stayed 95.86% in the 06:51 bucket (window mean 96.02%, min 93.87%) and evictions_per_min stayed ~3/min (3.14 at 06:51, window mean 2.99), matching the pre-onset 06:42 values (96.01%, 2.75).

portfolio-service — the only service deployed in the week (v4.4.0 at 05:50Z) and a co-consumer of redis-cache — shows no latency change at onset: p99 avg 180.28 ms in the 06:51 bucket vs 180.46 ms at 06:42, holding ~174-185 ms for the whole window (mean 180.23 ms).

The other two shared-redis consumers are also flat across onset: pricing-engine p99 avg 59.66 ms in the 06:51 bucket (window mean 59.89 ms) and market-data-service p99 avg 40.17 ms (window mean 39.90 ms), both unchanged from 06:42.

No dependency latency rise precedes or coincides with auth-service's onset: the shared redis-cache, its three co-consumers, and portfolio-service all remain at baseline in the 06:42 and 06:51 buckets while auth-service p99 rose from ~90 ms to 2532 ms in that same 06:51 bucket — so the dependency-first / shared-component-degradation candidates are not supported by the measured services.

user-db does not expose latency_p99_ms; its available metrics are connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min, so user-db latency/IOPS could not be compared against onset with this query.

The metric backend returns auth-service sub-buckets at bucket_seconds=120 (2-min resolution) — not the ~1-3 min finer resolution requested; all 4 series (request_rate, cpu_pct, rate_limited_per_min, latency_p99_ms) are on the same 120s grid with missing_points=0 and partial=false. So the ordering below is resolved at 2-min granularity.

auth-service inbound request_rate was flat at ~381-418 req/s for the entire baseline 06:00-06:48 (e.g. 06:42 avg 403.12, 06:44 avg 404.07, 06:48 avg 386.14). It did NOT rise before the CPU jump: at the 06:50 bucket it was still only 452.43 avg (max 529.5), and it inflected upward only in the 06:52 bucket (742.81) and after — 1094.83 at 06:54, 1350.36 at 06:56, peaking 1749.75 avg at 06:58.

auth-service per-service CPU jumped FIRST, in the 06:52 bucket: 96.89% avg / 96.96% max, from a flat ~34-40% baseline (06:50 bucket was 34.42 avg). It held 96.6-98.8% through 07:14 (07:12 max 98.84). The CPU step (06:52) and the request_rate step (06:52, 742.81) land in the SAME 2-min bucket — request rate did not precede CPU.

The p99 latency inflection is in the 06:54 bucket (3759.86 ms avg, 3849.2 max), i.e. AFTER both the CPU step and the request_rate step. The 06:50-06:52 buckets were still baseline-fast (93.94 ms avg at 06:50, 91.5 ms avg at 06:52); p99 stayed ~3.55-3.93 s from 06:54 through 07:14.

rate_limited_per_min is a genuine exposed auth-service metric (listed in available_metrics) and shows the same ordering: flat ~1.3-2.6 req/min through 06:52 (1.21 at 06:52), then a sharp rise only at 06:54 (451.86 avg, max 902.06) and ~868-920 req/min from 06:56 onward — it lags rather than leads the CPU step, consistent with the documented autoscaler cap (maxReplicas 8) rejecting surplus connections once CPU saturated. request_rate IS exposed, so it is the direct proxy; rate_limited_per_min corroborates.

Interpretation for the H1-vs-H2 test: within the 2-min resolution, request_rate did NOT rise before the ~38%->~97% CPU jump — CPU saturates in the 06:52 bucket side-by-side with the first request-rate uptick, and auth-service p99 only moves one bucket later (06:54). The elevated inbound rate itself is best read as a consequence of the already-slow service (retries/backlog: once p99 goes to ~3.76 s at 06:54, request_rate keeps climbing to 1749.75 at 06:58 and rate_limited caps at ~900/min), not as a pre-onset volume surge. This ordering is consistent with H1 (CPU cost per request rose on an unchanged ~400 req/s baseline) and is not explained by H2's premise of a login surge that outran capacity before the CPU climb.

SCALE CHECK: I searched for an earlier inflection in both components for 06:30-07:15 (or a longer baseline window) and found none preceding auth-service's onset; both components' first deviation is at/after the auth-service onset window, and the deviations are consistent with being downstream demand/symptom rather than the origin. GAP: I ran out of tool-call budget before inspecting any metric bucket earlier than 06:30 for these two components, so an inflection strictly before the auth-service onset bucket (06:42-06:51) is not excluded by direct measurement — only that no deviation appears in the 06:30-06:51 stretch.

findings.statement: user-db connections_active was FLAT through the auth-service onset, then doubled: it held 22.79-27.75 for every minute 06:30-06:51 (06:42=26.17, 06:51=26.39) and jumped to 72.59 at 06:52, staying 72.22-84.53 through 07:15 (e.g. 06:54=79.84, 07:01=84.53). The rise therefore begins one bucket AFTER auth-service's 06:51 onset (auth p99 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket), not before it.

user-db's other four metrics are flat across onset with no inflection: replication_lag_ms stayed 27.65-32.31 ms for all 46 minutes (06:42=31.44, 06:51=30.99, 06:52=30.47; mean 29.96), cpu_pct stayed 16.63-19.94% (06:42=16.98, 06:51=18.97, 06:52=19.24; mean 18.0), slow_queries_per_min stayed 0.18-0.51/min (06:42=0.22, 06:51=0.35, 07:10=0.51), and disk_used_pct stayed 43.41-44.87% (06:42=43.73, 06:51=43.9) — no saturation, lag spike, slow-query burst or disk exhaustion at or before 06:51.

findings.statement: api-gateway showed no resource saturation as the trigger: cpu_pct stayed 36.92-45.98% (mean 41.68) for the entire 06:30-07:15 window including the 4024 ms latency bucket (06:54=39.4, 06:55=36.92, 06:51=39.47), never approaching saturation. Note api-gateway's available_metrics are cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts — it exposes NO connection/queue-count metric, so the gateway's connection or accept-queue state could not be measured directly.

The api-gateway deviation sequence (latency 06:54, errors 06:55) lines up with auth-service's own saturation evidence rather than preceding it: auth-service's first 503 on /v1/auth/login is logged at 06:55:42 'accept queue full', and auth-service p99 was already 2532 ms in the 06:51 bucket — so gateway p99/errors rise 3-4 minutes AFTER auth-service's latency onset, consistent with the gateway propagating slowness/503s from auth-service. I did not have budget for api-gateway/user-db logs or API-point of-view 503 confirmation, so this ordering rests on metrics only.
